title: Operators and Expressions
subtitle: Evaluate arithmetic, comparison, assignment and logical expressions.
description: Practice numeric calculations and Boolean comparisons.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 3: Operators and Expressions. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Operators and Expressions”. The goal is to evaluate arithmetic, comparison, assignment and logical expressions.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Operators combine values into expressions. Arithmetic produces numeric results, comparison operators produce true/false results, and logical operators combine conditions.

blocks.title: Sample 1: Operators and Expressions in practice

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Evaluate arithmetic, comparison, assignment and logical expressions. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A division operation may receive a zero denominator. What is the best design?
options: Assume zero is impossible.
Check or otherwise handle the zero case before dividing.
Round the denominator to zero.
Hide the result when it is incorrect.
blocks.explanation: Guarding the denominator prevents a known invalid operation and lets the program give a useful response.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Guarding the denominator prevents a known invalid operation and lets the program give a useful response.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Guarding the denominator prevents a known invalid operation and lets the program give a useful response.

blocks.title: Sample 2: Operators and Expressions in practice

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real Swift project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A developer writes a complex condition with several AND/OR operators. What improves correctness most?
options: Remove all parentheses.
Convert each condition to text.
Repeat the expression in several places.
Use parentheses and descriptive intermediate values where they clarify the rule.
blocks.explanation: Explicit grouping and named conditions make logic easier to verify.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Explicit grouping and named conditions make logic easier to verify.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Explicit grouping and named conditions make logic easier to verify.

blocks.text: Precedence determines which operation is evaluated first, but parentheses are often worth adding when they make the intended meaning clearer. Do not confuse comparison with assignment: they answer different questions and often use different symbols.

blocks.title: Sample 3: Operators and Expressions in practice

blocks.question: A value comparison unexpectedly treats a decimal as slightly different from the expected value. What should be considered?
options: Floating-point values can have representation/rounding effects.
All decimals are exact in every language.
Comparison operators never return false.
The output font changed the value.
blocks.explanation: Binary floating-point cannot represent every decimal exactly; rounding or tolerance may be appropriate for the domain.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Binary floating-point cannot represent every decimal exactly; rounding or tolerance may be appropriate for the domain.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Binary floating-point cannot represent every decimal exactly; rounding or tolerance may be appropriate for the domain.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning

Check edge cases such as division by zero, integer division, floating-point rounding, and comparing values that may be absent. A mathematically plausible expression can still be wrong for the data type or domain you are using.

blocks.title: Sample 4: Operators and Expressions in practice

blocks.text: Before continuing, explain in your own words how this topic helps solve the dashboard goal: Practice numeric calculations and Boolean comparisons. Try one boundary case, one normal case, and one case that should be rejected or handled differently.

blocks.question: A price calculation mixes addition and multiplication. How can the developer make the intended order obvious?
options: Rely on memory and remove spaces.
Move the calculation into a loop.
Use parentheses to express the intended grouping.
Convert every number to text.
blocks.explanation: Parentheses make grouping explicit and reduce precedence mistakes.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Parentheses make grouping explicit and reduce precedence mistakes.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Parentheses make grouping explicit and reduce precedence mistakes.

blocks.question: A condition should check whether a score is at least 50. Which comparison expresses that requirement?
options: score >= 50
score = 50
score < 50
score + 50
blocks.explanation: The greater-than-or-equal comparison includes 50 and every larger value.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The greater-than-or-equal comparison includes 50 and every larger value.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. The greater-than-or-equal comparison includes 50 and every larger value.
